query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A DFT-guided surface modification that adjusts the local surface potential of stainless steel can induce the formation of a robust, self-healing passivation layer, thereby enhancing its corrosion resistance under extreme conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel with its standard, inadequately performing oxide/passivation layer in extreme corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface treatment strategy—such as a thin film deposition or doping process—designed using DFT simulations to modify and optimize the surface potential.
generation.conditions: Exposure to extreme corrosive environments, for example high-chloride, high-temperature, or molten salt conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A redefined surface layer enriched in noble elements that acts as a protective passivation barrier.
generation.mechanism: The computationally tailored surface potential promotes the formation of a stable, self-healing passivation (oxide) layer, which impedes ion dissolution and retards the progression of corrosion reactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the corrosion rate of the modified stainless steel compared to the untreated baseline, as evidenced by lower weight loss and improved electrochemical performance.
generation.baseline: Stainless steel in its conventional passivated state without DFT-guided modification.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be observed within the design limits of the engineered passivation layer; under conditions exceeding these limits (e.g., extreme thermal or chemical stress beyond the optimized range), the performance gain may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement and long-term stability of the engineered layer in diverse extreme conditions are yet to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless steel samples: one set with the DFT-guided surface modification and one untreated control. Expose both sets to a defined extreme corrosive condition (e.g., high-chloride or molten salt environment at elevated temperatures) for an extended period. Routinely monitor the samples for corrosion-related degradation.
measurements: Weight loss measurements to quantify corrosion rate
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) to verify the formation and composition of the passivation layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower corrosion rates and more robust/passivating surface features) compared to the controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6
